title: The Schools Where Good Teaching Matters Most
author: Dylan Kane
summary: Dylan Kane offers a mental model for why teaching is harder in some schools than others without blaming circumstances or adults. Students vary randomly in cognitive resources such as working memory capacity and processing speed, and students with fewer of them are more sensitive to instructional quality, needing practice, small steps, managed attention, explicit connections, sequencing, modeling, review and fading scaffolds. Compensating factors such as outside tutoring, prior knowledge and contagious motivation can offset fewer resources. Poverty shifts the distribution by sapping cognitive resources through stress, instability and deprivation, so in high-poverty schools more students need excellent instruction, fewer get outside help, gaps compound and motivation can spread downward. He warns that high test scores in affluent schools often reflect demographics rather than teaching quality, and that schools succeeding with high-poverty students look more structured and intense. His conclusion is that managing cognitive load is the real answer, but it is content-specific and still largely an unsolved problem.
points: Students with more cognitive resources can learn from mediocre instruction, while students with fewer need excellent instruction that reduces working-memory load.
Outside instruction, prior knowledge and peer motivation compensate for lower cognitive resources, which is why affluent schools often look effective.
Poverty-related stress and deprivation erode cognitive resources, and gaps in prior knowledge compound over the years.
High achievement is frequently a product of demographics, so a school can look effective while failing students on the left of the distribution.
Managing cognitive load is subject-specific, and for most K-12 topics there is no accepted guidance, which makes it an unsolved problem.
quotes: Students with more cognitive resources are not very sensitive to the quality of instruction: even with mediocre instruction, they are still likely to learn. Students with fewer cognitive resources are much more sensitive to the quality of instruction
Cognitive resources don’t say anything about what students can or cannot learn, but they do influence the way that information needs to be delivered in order for learning to happen.
Memory is the residue of thought; students learn what they think about.
The best way to bypass the limitations of working memory and processing speed is to know a lot about a topic: that knowledge reduces the strain on working memory.

Some will make a kind of devil’s bargain, lowering expectations because it seems like the only way forward, but end up in a spiral of lower rigor that erodes the education of even the students who have more cognitive resources.
In most cases, that high achievement is a result of demographics and not teaching quality. Pretty much any form of teaching will be successful with some students.
One tough consequence of this mental model is that schools that are successful working with a high-poverty student population look different. There is more structure. The teaching is intense.
I can’t google, “I’m teaching adding and subtracting decimals and I want to know how to teach it while managing cognitive load.” There’s no easy answer, no expert consensus.
